meaning: 'Unfailing Accomplishment' — the fifth Dhyānibuddha, lord of the karma family

phonemes.desc: The canonical restored form Amoghasiddhi — a Sanskrit compound of amogha, 'unfailing', and siddhi, 'accomplishment'.

pronunciation.approximation: Say 'amoghasiddhi' with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration 'Amoghasiddhi'.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: amogha, 'unfailing, not vain' — the negated adjective of mogha, 'useless, fruitless' (Monier-Williams s.v.).

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: siddhi, 'accomplishment, attainment, success' — from the root sādh, 'to accomplish', whence also sādhana, 'the means of accomplishment'.

kin.label: Cousin words
kin.form: siddha, 'the perfected one', and sādhaka, 'the practitioner' — the whole family of finishing what is begun.

pronunciation.note: The ASCII form 'amoghasiddhi' is a DNS compromise; the restoration 'Amoghasiddhi' preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

domains.title: Amoghasiddhi
domains.subtitle: Infallible Success
domains.lead: Amoghasiddhi — 'Unfailing Accomplishment' — is the fifth of the Five Meditation Buddhas (Dhyānibuddhas), lord of the karma family and sovereign of the mandala's northern quarter. Where his companions preside over insight, anger, pride, and desire, he presides over action itself: the wisdom that completes what is begun. His raised palm answers fear; his green body, the color of ripening, promises that no honest effort is wasted.

cards.name: The Karma Family
cards.desc: Lord of the karma family and bearer of all-accomplishing wisdom — the knowledge that finishes what is begun.

cards.name: The North and the Green
cards.desc: He occupies the northern quarter of the mandala, body the color of dusk-lit emerald, his element the wind that carries the deed.

cards.name: The Gesture of Fearlessness
cards.desc: His right hand raised in abhaya mudrā — the open palm that answers fear with the promise that no effort is wasted.

cards.name: Envy Transmuted
cards.desc: The affliction of envy — frozen, comparative, sterile — becomes under his gaze the energy of benevolent action for others.

symbols.name: The double vajra (viśvavajra)
symbols.meaning: The crossed thunderbolt stamped on his throne base — unshakeable means, doubled for the four directions, the karma family's seal.

symbols.name: The abhaya mudrā
symbols.meaning: The raised right hand, palm outward: fearlessness offered as a teaching, not brandished as a triumph.

symbols.name: The garuḍa throne-bearers
symbols.meaning: The sovereign birds that carry his seat in the iconographic manuals — emblems of power subdued and enlisted.

symbols.name: Green
symbols.meaning: His body-color in the five-Buddha system: the hue of ripening action, of autumn and of deeds coming to fruit.

symbols.name: The wind (vāyu)
symbols.meaning: His element — movement and transmission, the deed carried outward to its object; he is the least static of the five.

symbols.name: Samayatārā and Viśvapāṇi
symbols.meaning: His consort, the Green Tārā, and his bodhisattva Viśvapāṇi, 'he whose hand is everywhere' — pledge and method made persons.

mythology.lead: Amoghasiddhi has no biographical myths — he was never born, never walked the earth, never died. He belongs to the tantric synthesis of the early medieval period, when Mahāyāna Buddhism organized its meditation Buddhas into a mandala of five. His stories are the ritual and iconographic programs that grew around his name from the eighth century on, above all in the Sarva-tathāgata-tattva-saṅgraha, the root tantra of the system.

myths.title: The Fifth from the One
myths.text: The Sarva-tathāgata-tattva-saṅgraha — 'The Compendium of the Reality of All the Thus-Gones' — is the great tantra of the late eighth century from which the five-Buddha system descends. It organizes the Buddhas as a mandala: Vairocana at the center, and four Jinas in the quarters — Akṣobhya east, Ratnasambhava south, Amitābha west, Amoghasiddhi north. Each rules a family (kula) and transmutes a poison into its mirror-virtue: anger becomes mirror-like wisdom, pride becomes equality, desire becomes discernment, and, for Amoghasiddhi, envy becomes all-accomplishing wisdom (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna). Note what his name does that the others' do not: while Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amitābha are described by what they are — unshakable, jewel-born, infinite light — Amoghasiddhi is described by what he does. The name is the system's only promise: it does not fail.

myths.title: The Subduing of Maheśvara
myths.text: The tantra stages its founding drama in the karma family's own theater. The worldly gods, led by Maheśvara — Śiva enthroned on Mount Meru with his consort and his host — defy the Buddha's law and oppress the beings under their rule. Vajrapāṇi, first among the karma-family beings, descends to the summit, binds Maheśvara with his noose, and tramples him underfoot; and where a lesser story would end in destruction, this one ends in conscription — the conquered god accepts initiation and becomes a guardian of the very mandala that broke him (STTS; Snellgrove, Indo-Tibetan Buddhism, reads the episode as the tantric appropriation of Śiva). It is a theological conquest, not a defeat: the powers of the older religion are neither destroyed nor tolerated but converted into doorkeepers. The karma family's first recorded action is the transformation of an enemy into a function.

myths.title: The Hand That Answers Fear
myths.text: Amoghasiddhi's right hand is raised, palm outward — the abhaya mudrā, the gesture of fearlessness. The iconographic manuals of Nepal and Tibet prescribe it for him alone of the five, with the left hand resting in the lap, and the Vinaya tradition supplied the gesture's biography: when Devadatta loosed the maddened elephant Nālāgiri against the Buddha, the beast came trumpeting down the road of Rājagṛha and knelt before the raised hand, tamed by an empty palm (Cullavagga 7.4; the Dhammapada commentary tells it fully). Later commentators attached the same gesture to Amoghasiddhi's northern quarter, the karma family, whose whole business is action in a frightened world. The meaning is exact and inverse to what we expect of power: a Buddha does not answer threat by closing his fist but by opening his hand — and the threat disarms itself. Fearlessness, in this iconography, is not the absence of danger but the refusal to return it.

myths.title: The North, the Wind, and Green
myths.text: The iconographic manuals complete him. Green, the color of ripening action; the wind (vāyu) as his element, the deed carried to its object; autumn as his season, the harvest of effort; a throne borne by garuḍas, the sovereign birds; his consort Samayatārā — the great Green Tārā herself absorbed into the family scheme — and his bodhisattva Viśvapāṇi, 'he whose hand is everywhere'; his northern paradise named, in the ritual texts, Karmaprasiddhi, the fulfillment of action. In the painted mandalas of the Kathmandu Valley and Tibet he sits at the northern gate of the assembly, and it is his family — karma, action — that governs the rites by which the practitioner consecrates the ground, draws the lines, and performs the offerings. Everything about him is oriented toward completion. Where the western Jinas preside over seeing and becoming, the northern one presides over finishing: Amoghasiddhi is the Buddha of the finished work.

lore.syncretism: Amoghasiddhi's closest relative is Śiva, in a relationship of deliberate supersession: the root tantra has Vajrapāṇi of the karma family subdue Maheśvara on Mount Meru and trample him into the mandala as its guardian — conquest written as conversion. In East Asia the five-Buddha mandala traveled with esoteric Buddhism: in the Shingon school of Japan, Amoghasiddhi appears as Fukūjōju Nyorai, the 'Tathāgata of Infallible Success', enthroned in the north of the Diamond-Realm mandala preserved in the ninth-century scrolls of Tō-ji. His consort Samayatārā is simply the Green Tārā absorbed into the five-Buddha family scheme, so that the most beloved goddess of Tibetan devotion is also, doctrinally, his wisdom made feminine. Modern Western reception has been quieter than for his companions: he is known chiefly through museum galleries and meditation literature, where his name circulates as a compact promise — that accomplishment pursued without vanity does not fail.
lore.culturalLegacy: Amoghasiddhi's legacy is liturgical rather than narrative, and vast in that register. He presides over the top registers of countless Nepalese paubha paintings and Tibetan thangkas, where his image is among the most standardized in Himalayan art — green, right hand raised, seated on a throne borne by garuḍas. In Japan the esoteric schools chant his mantra within the Kongōkai mandala rites performed at Tō-ji and Kōya-san since the ninth century, and Fukūjōju remains a familiar presence in temple statuary from Nara to Kamakura. His doctrine survives as a compact psychology: envy — the conviction that others accomplish while I do not — is transmuted into all-accomplishing action, because karma performed for others cannot fail. In contemporary dharma centers his name is invoked less often than Tārā's, but it answers a question hers does not: whether the effort itself is worth anything. His name is the vow that it is.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Every tradition personifies its favorite anxiety. The Greeks made a goddess of ruin, the Norse of old age; Buddhism personified the fear of wasted effort. Amoghasiddhi is the answer to the question every practitioner asks in the dark middle of the work: is any of this actually working? His name is the vow — not vain, not useless, infallible.

Look at what his assigned affliction is: envy, the poison of comparison, the certainty that accomplishment lives in other people's hands. His teaching does not suppress that energy; it redirects it, because all-accomplishing wisdom acts for others, and action done selflessly for others cannot fail — there is no one left for it to fail in front of. The raised hand is not a trophy. It is a promise made to the frightened, by the one Buddha whose name is not a description but a guarantee.
lore.archaeology: There are no ancient temples of Amoghasiddhi, no inscriptions naming him, no early coins: he appears first in manuscript and image. Palm-leaf copies of the Sarva-tathāgata-tattva-saṅgraha survive among the Newar Buddhist manuscripts of the Kathmandu Valley, and his figure becomes canonical in paubha painting from the twelfth century and in Tibetan thangkas from the thirteenth, where the five Buddhas crown the registers of monastery murals across the Himalaya. In East Asia the ninth-century Tō-ji mandala scrolls preserve him as Fukūjōju in the Kongōkai, among the oldest monumental images of the system. His material record is therefore neither a site nor a relic but a genre — the painted mandala, portable and reproducible, in which the north never lacks its green Buddha.

sources: Guhyasamāja Tantra, ch. III — the earliest systematic tantric mandala of the five Dhyānibuddhas, naming Amoghasiddhi in the northern seat of the karma family.

Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha (Tattvasaṃgraha Tantra) — the paradigmatic narrative of the five tathāgatas' subjugation of the unruly forces, with Amoghasiddhi presiding over the north, the wind element, and all-accomplishing wisdom.
Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, v. 8 — the liturgical verse naming the five tathāgatas (Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi) that underlies the whole pentad system.

Alice Getty, The Gods of Northern Buddhism: Their History, Iconography and Progressive Evolution through the Northern Buddhist Countries (Oxford University Press, 1914) — the classic iconographic reference for Amoghasiddhi's green body, abhaya mudrā, and double-vajra throne.
Benoytosh Bhattacharyya, An Introduction to Buddhist Esoterism (Oxford University Press, 1932) — early scholarly exposition of the five Dhyānibuddhas and the karma family.

David L. Snellgrove, Indo-Tibetan Buddhism: Indian Buddhists & Their Tibetan Successors (Shambhala, 1987) — standard modern account of the tantric Buddha-family system from which Amoghasiddhi's iconography derives.
